object_entity.notes: North African council convened under Cyprian c. 251 after the Decian persecution to establish policy on the readmission of the lapsed; distinguished categories of lapse and mandated graded penance under episcopal authority; opposed both the rigorist position (Novatian) and the lax granting of peace by confessors.

context_place.notes: Major North African city; center of Latin Christianity from Tertullian through Cyprian and Augustine; seat of important regional councils.

evidence.notes: Cyprian presided over the council reflected in De Lapsis.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: But to those who have stood firm and have not been overthrown, what great joy! To those who have lapsed, medicine is not to be denied; but the lapsed must not assume that peace can be given them hastily by anyone. Let them knock at the door of the Church, but not with violence to break it down; let them beg but not presumptuously demand. Proper penance under the bishop's authority must precede reconciliation.
passage.notes: Graded penance under episcopal authority; against hasty reconciliation by confessors

object_entity.event_label: Council of Carthage (252) on Infant Baptism
object_entity.notes: North African council convened under Cyprian c. 252 responding to Bishop Fidus's question about delaying infant baptism until the eighth day; the council unanimously ruled that baptism should not be delayed — infants may be baptized as early as the second or third day after birth; key witness for infant baptism as assumed standard practice.

context_place.notes: Major North African city; center of Latin Christianity from Tertullian through Cyprian and Augustine; seat of important regional councils.

evidence.notes: Cyprian reports the council's unanimous ruling in Ep. 64.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: But in respect of the case of infants, which you say ought not to be baptized within the second or third day after their birth, and that the old law of circumcision should be regarded, so that you think one who is just born should not be baptized and sanctified within the eighth day — we all thought very differently in our council. For in this course which you thought was to be taken, no one agreed; but we all rather judged that the mercy and grace of God ought to be denied to no man born.
passage.notes: Council of Carthage 252 ruling: infant baptism not to be delayed; grace denied to none

object_entity.notes: Council held September 1, 256 under Cyprian's presidency with 87 North African bishops present; each bishop individually declared heretical baptism invalid and mandated rebaptism of converts from heretical groups; the fullest surviving example of North African collegial episcopal practice; opposed by Pope Stephen I of Rome.

context_place.notes: Major North African city; center of Latin Christianity from Tertullian through Cyprian and Augustine; seat of important regional councils.

evidence.notes: Cyprian presides and speaks in the Sententiae proem.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Cyprian said: You have heard, most beloved colleagues, what Jubaianus our fellow bishop wrote to me, consulting my moderate ability about the unlawful and profane baptism of heretics, and what I wrote back to him. Let each of us now bring forward what we think on this matter, judging no man nor rejecting any from the right of communion if he should think differently from us. For none of us sets himself up as a bishop of bishops or by tyrannical terror forces his colleagues to obedience.
passage.notes: Episcopal collegiality; no bishop of bishops; conciliar freedom of conscience

object_entity.notes: Student of Origen; bishop of Alexandria c. 248–264; key figure in the Trinitarian controversies after Origen; opposed Sabellianism but was himself accused of tritheism; major voice during the Decian persecution and the Novatian controversy; extensive correspondence preserved by Eusebius.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Eusebius notes that Firmilian of Caesarea in Cappadocia strongly supported Cyprian's position and wrote a sharp letter (preserved as Ep. 75 in Cyprian's collection) criticizing Stephen's appeal to Peter's chair, arguing that Stephen was in fact the schismatic for threatening to break communion. Dionysius of Alexandria also wrote to Stephen urging moderation and peace.

He threatened to break communion with the African churches.
passage.notes: Stephen's position: tradition forbids rebaptism; laying on of hands sufficient for reconciliation
